The Texas Senate race is shaping up to be a colossal collision of opposing forces: a young, social-media-savvy Democrat against the state’s well-known (but not necessarily well-liked) Republican attorney general.

   Democrat James Talarico is flooding the Texas airwaves with ads and raising money all over the place. Talarico appears to be more of a natural campaigner than Republican Ken Paxton, though Paxton has run—and won—plenty of times in Texas before.

   But it’s a race. Republican Sen. John Cornyn, whose seat the two are fighting over, has had harsh words for Paxton, calling him “lazy” and a “poor campaigner.” Paxton’s campaign posted a rather low-energy video of him over the weekend, which led to plenty of online mockery.

   Talarico, though, has said plenty of controversial things, including at one point saying “God is nonbinary.” Do voters really know him? Will he run through the tape, or fade like plenty of other Democrats have done in the past?

   A recent poll from the University of Texas has Talarico up three points, 42% to 39%, in the Senate race, which would be an absolute steal for Democrats as they attempt to reclaim the Senate. 

   But Democrats shouldn’t get their cowboy hats out just yet. 

   • Democrats haven’t won a statewide seat in Texas since 1994, the year “The Lion King” was released. That was 13 years before the first iPhone was released in the United States. That’s a lot of losing. Republicans are holding a midterm convention in Dallas in September, where they can bring the GOP’s muscle to Paxton home turf. It’s a big opportunity for him, if he takes advantage of it.

   • In an interview Sunday , Paxton acknowledged the race is tight, but he said his attempt to define Talarico for Texas voters is about to be unleashed. “The voters just don’t know yet because we have not been up on TV. But that’s coming,” he told Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich. But has Paxton waited too long? He seems financially outmatched by Talarico at this point.

   • Paxton needs money. Sen. John Kennedy (R., La.) told Fox News that Senate Republicans hadn’t budgeted a ton of money for Paxton’s campaign, and they would rely on President Trump for that. That will be up to Trump and his enormous campaign war chest.

Damian Paletta
 
Ken Paxton Is in Texas Trouble, But He Has History (and Trump)
 
Plus, how U.S. tariffs could hurt Canadian small businesses, and Congress might work on shoring up Social Security
 
 
BRANDON BELL/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. The Texas Senate race is shaping up to be a colossal collision of opposing forces: a young, social-media-savvy Democrat against the state’s well-known (but not necessarily well-liked) Republican attorney general.

 

Democrat James Talarico is flooding the Texas airwaves with ads and raising money all over the place. Talarico appears to be more of a natural campaigner than Republican Ken Paxton, though Paxton has run—and won—plenty of times in Texas before.

 

But it’s a race. Republican Sen. John Cornyn, whose seat the two are fighting over, has had harsh words for Paxton, calling him “lazy” and a “poor campaigner.” Paxton’s campaign posted a rather low-energy video of him over the weekend, which led to plenty of online mockery.

 

Talarico, though, has said plenty of controversial things, including at one point saying “God is nonbinary.” Do voters really know him? Will he run through the tape, or fade like plenty of other Democrats have done in the past?

 

A recent poll from the University of Texas has Talarico up three points, 42% to 39%, in the Senate race, which would be an absolute steal for Democrats as they attempt to reclaim the Senate. 

 

But Democrats shouldn’t get their cowboy hats out just yet. 

 

• Democrats haven’t won a statewide seat in Texas since 1994, the year “The Lion King” was released. That was 13 years before the first iPhone was released in the United States. That’s a lot of losing. Republicans are holding a midterm convention in Dallas in September, where they can bring the GOP’s muscle to Paxton home turf. It’s a big opportunity for him, if he takes advantage of it.

 

• In an interview Sunday, Paxton acknowledged the race is tight, but he said his attempt to define Talarico for Texas voters is about to be unleashed. “The voters just don’t know yet because we have not been up on TV. But that’s coming,” he told Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich. But has Paxton waited too long? He seems financially outmatched by Talarico at this point.

 

• Paxton needs money. Sen. John Kennedy (R., La.) told Fox News that Senate Republicans hadn’t budgeted a ton of money for Paxton’s campaign, and they would rely on President Trump for that. That will be up to Trump and his enormous campaign war chest.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

U.S.-Iran conflict: Tensions are high in the region after U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. The renewed fighting sent oil prices up.

 

Trump’s Monday: The president is scheduled at take part in a policy meeting at 2 p.m. At 3 p.m., he is scheduled to make an announcement on healthcare affordability.

What I’m Following

 
 
CARLOS OSORIO/REUTERS
 

Canadian small businesses will feel the sting from new tariffs. The Canadian economy as a whole is projected to withstand the new tariffs of 50% on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, or about 5% of Canada’s U.S.-bound exports. But many small and medium-size Canadian business owners are expected to bear the brunt of the pain, and some fear they could be put out of business without a resolution.

 

Social Security moves to the front burner for Congress. Social Security’s looming insolvency is the country’s most foreseeable problem, threatening automatic benefit cuts in 2032. Discussions on the issue accelerated this summer, and analysts anticipate Republicans and Democrats to hold hands eventually and jump to prevent benefit cuts for tens of millions of seniors and perhaps address the program’s long-term health.

 

Opportunity Zone investors are bracing for the tax bill to arrive. Investors in the Opportunity Zone program—the first Trump administration’s tax incentive to push capital into low-income areas—approach a critical date Dec. 31. That’s when they must include long-deferred capital gains in taxable income. The ticking clock has set off a planning flurry as advisers try to help their mostly high-income clients minimize the hit.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Japan plans to shift more of its military spending toward drones and missiles and build up supplies of ammunition, but the pace of spending increases might be too slow for Washington.

 

• The head of the G20’s Financial Stability Board wrote in a letter Monday that new AI models are a growing threat to the stability of the global financial system.

 

• Russian officials have long described the war as one against the “collective West,” not just Ukraine.

 

• Icelanders voted against restarting negotiations on joining the European Union in a nationwide referendum.
